brief_angle: When a museum deletes its wall labels, does the information actually disappear or just migrate — and does the deaf visitor end up in a more level room, or in a room whose default channel has quietly become speech (docents, tours, audio guides) with text demoted to atmosphere?
notes: APHORISM DENSITY: you are over budget on verdict-sentences and they are cannibalizing each other. 'Text demoted to atmosphere. Speech promoted to default.' (para 4); 'My argument broke against a phone.' (para 6); 'Same century, opposite decisions.' (para 7); 'That is the load-bearing wall.' (para 11). Keep ONE. 'My argument broke against a phone.' is the strongest because it also carries the discovery — flatten the other three into plain prose so it lands alone.

SIGNPOSTED MOVES: 'Now the position I actually have to fight.' (opening the docent-acoustics paragraph) announces the technique. Delete that sentence and let the objection start with 'Someone will tell me the room itself is the political layer.' The paragraph works fine standing on its own; the announcement just tells me a requirement is being satisfied.

MANAGING THE READER / QUOTED VOICE, and a fix that solves both: the Christine Sun Kim material is your strongest complication but there is no real quoted voice in the whole piece — the museum spokesperson line and Kim's captions are the only quotes, and Kim never speaks in her own past-tense words. More urgently, 'So the label was never the point. What the label carried was the point' (para after Kim) is you stepping in to explain the juxtaposition the Kim example already makes. Cut that explanatory sentence; the contrast between Kim tearing off the neutral label and Calder deleting both carries itself. And note for protection: the Kim thread is a genuine COMPLICATING EXAMPLE from inside your own value system — it currently stays unresolved, which is right. Do not tidy it.
